title: Cuzco
capsule: Qusqu (Cusco), in the Andes of southern Peru, was the seat of the small Inca polity known as the Kingdom of Cusco before its mid-15th-century transformation into the empire of Tawantinsuyu. Through the dynasty traditionally listed from Manco Capac to Viracocha Inca, the city-state remained one of several competing Andean chiefdoms, expanding gradually while contending with neighboring peoples such as the Ayarmaca, the Cunti, and the Chanka. According to Inca tradition, this formative kingdom period ended around 1438, when Cusi Yupanqui repelled the Chanka invasion, took the name Pachacuti, and launched the imperial expansion and monumental rebuilding of Cusco that would follow. The city's strategic position between the Huatanay and Tullumayo rivers anchored both the modest kingdom and the empire it became.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Cusco's urban and political history from the fifteenth century onward is well documented through Spanish colonial records and extensive archaeology; the earlier pre-Pachacuti Killke-period polity's territorial extent before c. 1400 is based on limited excavation rather than mapped boundaries.
